text:
Michael Saylor says the Clarity Act stalling was the best thing that could have happened to crypto. It killed 600 pages of restrictions, and the regulators filled the gap with friendlier guidance.

From his Bloomberg TV interview this week:

"So we have very pro digital assets regulators. Within a week of Clarity stalling, we got positive guidance from Treasury, from the CFTC, and from the SEC.

The CFTC gave very good guidance for crypto derivatives. The SEC gave good guidance for tokenizing securities. Treasury gave good guidance for digital currencies.

The Clarity Act had 600 pages of restrictions in it. And so while it would de facto or de jure legitimize the industry, it did it with 600 pages of restrictions. When Clarity stalled, the restrictions went away, and the guidance that came out is actually much better for the industry.

So the reason the industry is rallying and the reason Bitcoin is rallying is because Bitcoin doesn't need the law, and the rules coming out of the administration are actually progressive, pro digital assets, and I think that they'll catalyze a wave of growth in the industry.

And I think Clarity stalling was the best thing that could have happened to our industry."

text:
my conviction on @Kinetiq_xyz is purely a bet on @0xOmnia and the team delivering a pristine experience with @Enter_Elysium.

the progress so far is quite satisfying. there's a wave of protocols steering the ship towards the ecosystem. no big protocols yet, but I feel that's the beauty of it.

maybe a bit weird, but if we're looking into mythology, Elysium is the place of absolute peace, free from the struggles of the normal world.

besides the struggles of HyperEVM that the Kinetiq team fixes with the launch of Elysium, there's another important aspect that I think will make sense in the grand scheme of things.

any chain that launches goes through these phases of cannibalization and economic parasitism. all the protocols launching in that specific ecosystem have a single motivation: compete for users and liquidity, rise to the top and create the most value for your token.

there's nothing wrong with this per se, but it is why PvE turns into PvP so quickly, as the resources on any chain will eventually become finite. let's not even touch on the vast number of L2s which give crumbs back to the actual L1 as they achieve structural decoupling.

Elysium seems to be designed around the exact opposite idea.

instead of creating another sovereign economy that slowly decouples from the layer underneath it, its success is still structurally tied to the success of Hyperliquid.

$HYPE remains the native gas asset. applications on Elysium are meant to interact with HyperCore liquidity rather than recreate it somewhere else. more activity on Elysium can therefore translate into more market making, arbitrage, hedging and ultimately more volume flowing through HyperCore.

the L2 doesn't need Hyperliquid to lose for Elysium to win.

quite the opposite.

if Elysium becomes a better execution environment for applications that simply cannot operate efficiently on HyperEVM today, it expands the surface area of what can be built around Hyperliquid while keeping the economic gravity centred around the same ecosystem.

and this simple reflexivity is also reaching other builders, the ones which are not trying to compete purely in their own interest on Elysium, but actually the ones giving back to the Elysium ecosystem and the Kinetiq community.

it's through protocols like @AscendLaunch, @NestExchange or @MontraXYZ, which have already announced that they will use part of their fees to buy back kinetiq:native tokens and burn them, in a similar process to what the Hyperliquid Foundation is doing.

and imagine if you get 10-20 protocols doing the same, working together to push the chain further. what will this attract in the end?

a stronger community, more activity, more interest from developers, making Elysium a more attractive place to launch your protocol and work together to build something great.

simply put, a high-throughput utopian world.

i strongly believe we are about to see a new standard being set for how any ecosystem should operate and how the force and alignment of the builders inside the ecosystem can create a halo effect.

text:
Ali Ghodsi of @Databricks on the four conditions that would have to hold for AI to truly improve itself:

"The next model requires less resources, less GPUs to train... The second condition: the next model takes less time to train as well. Third, accuracy of the model, the intelligence is increasing. And fourth, we can do the former three again and again and again... All at the same time, not just any of them."

"If you just mean that the software is writing itself, we're already there today. Like 90-some percent of the software in Databricks is written by AI. Does it matter if the last few percent is also written by AI? No."

"If you're getting these four conditions, then you might get a speed-up where the next model, let's say, takes half amount of time and half the resources, and it is more intelligent... By the way, I don't even know if that necessarily leads you to superintelligence."

"A lot of people, their definition is just, 'Hey, if I'm not even coding anymore and it's coding itself'... I think they're conflating, 'Hey, what's my value and is it scary for me?' Versus, 'Hey, that then means we'll get that superintelligence that in 2014 was hypothesized by Bostrom.'"

@alighodsi @martin_casado @sarah_wang

text:
🥷Neurai: Silent Payments
Silent payments are based on Bitcoin BIP-352, which, by leveraging Taproot’s capabilities, allows someone to share a special address for receiving funds, an address that changes for each transaction received.

This allows someone who wants to receive regular payments to avoid exposing an address that could link them to other payments and compromise their privacy on the network.

We have adapted this method for Neurai, and since we do not have Taproot, we have adapted the Silent Payments to Authscript. 

Adding this capability to our network is possible thanks to the advanced scripts we’ve been implementing over the past few months, which allow the network to operate in multiple ways, bringing us closer to Ethereum in terms of utility.

Privacy is something we take very seriously, which is why we’ve been adding privacy-related features such as the privacy pool and DePIN messaging via Assets. But we also believe this should be optional, for those who need it, allowing our network to accommodate both approaches.

#Neurai #XNA neurai:native #Privacy #BIP352

quoted_text:
i am bullish privacy and of course ethereum:0xe76c6c83af64e4c60245d8c7de953df673a7a33d, so i wanted to see how privacy competitors like ethereum:0xa12cc123ba206d4031d1c7f6223d1c2ec249f4f3 and solana:PRVT6TB7uss3FrUd2D9xs2zqDBsa3GbMJMwCQsgmeta stack up on my fundamental crypto asset scoreboard.

---

let's start with @zama:

short answer is (unfortunately), like many crypto projects, it is great tech with a weak token.

zama is one of the leading FHE stacks with:

> $647.9M of all-time shielded volume
> $127.5M of shielded TVL
> $104M earning yield in confidential morpho vaults

but almost none of that reaches the token yet.

every protocol fee is paid in ZAMA and burned. the burn is live onchain with 91,064 ZAMA burned on july 17 and another 73,300 waiting for the next batch.

that works out to ~$22.5k a year of burns against an $865M FDV, or ~38,500x.

the supply is also growing a lot faster than it burns. staking mints ~5% a year and the foundation releases 114.6M ZAMA a month from treasury and growth.

net of burns, that's a -19.8% DAAY (dilution-adjusted accrual yield). and even if the foundation holds every tranche, it's -5.7%.

only 22.4% of supply circulates, and the first team and investor cliff hits feb. 2, 2027 (550M ZAMA, ~22% of circulating), then ~302M a month after that.

so even if burns grow 90x to $2M a year by next october, the base case is $0.017, 78% below where it trades today.

working backwards, today's price at fair value needs burns to go from $22.5k to ~$85M a year within 5 years. that's 3,800x, or roughly 5x every year.

in comparison, ethereum:0xe76c6c83af64e4c60245d8c7de953df673a7a33d does ~$4.69M a year in fees on a ~$152M FDV, and nearly all of it reaches stakers through the treasury. that's ~200x the fees at about a sixth of the size.

---

now let's take a look at @UmbraPrivacy:

umbra launched through @MetaDAOProject last october, raising $3M at $0.30 against $155M of commitments.

that makes it an ownership token. the treasury, the mint authority, and the IP all sit with a futarchy-controlled DAO, so the team runs on a $100k/month budget and anything above that needs a DAO-approved proposal.

so structurally, solana:PRVT6TB7uss3FrUd2D9xs2zqDBsa3GbMJMwCQsgmeta gives tokenholders a lot more than ethereum:0xa12cc123ba206d4031d1c7f6223d1c2ec249f4f3 does. the problem is there isn't much to own yet besides the cash.

v1 shielding was free and shielded TVL is only ~$100K.

the first fee sources only went live this week:
> v2 (still invite-only)
> the uUSDv stablecoin (umbra keeps 25% of the yield)

the treasury holds ~$1.4M of stablecoins, or ~$0.06 per outstanding token. at $0.46, solana:PRVT6TB7uss3FrUd2D9xs2zqDBsa3GbMJMwCQsgmeta trades at ~7.8x that, so the market is paying ~$9.5M for a business with no revenue yet.

it has also funded operations by selling treasury tokens, ~3.2M UMBRA over the past year or ~13.5% of outstanding supply. net of a small buyback, that's a -12.1% DAAY.

the positive is that insider tokens only unlock at price targets (2x to 32x the ICO price), and nothing unlocks for at least 6 months.

my base case values the business at ~$6M, roughly where the ICO priced it, plus the cash. that gets to $0.23, ~50% below today after a +136% month.

---

final scores at a 6-month time horizon:

> ethereum:0xe76c6c83af64e4c60245d8c7de953df673a7a33d: 3.0, neutral
> solana:PRVT6TB7uss3FrUd2D9xs2zqDBsa3GbMJMwCQsgmeta: 2.3, underperform
> ethereum:0xa12cc123ba206d4031d1c7f6223d1c2ec249f4f3: 2.2, underperform

FHE and privacy on solana could still become a big part of onchain privacy, but the tokens need to start capturing usage to be valuable.

text:
Ethereum core devs were right to ship Glamsterdam with a deposit edge case they already know about.
Here's the edge case, raised by @LidoFinance on Thursday's ACDC #189 call.

Validator deposits have one old rule: first deposit wins.
The first pending deposit for a public key sets its withdrawal credentials forever, and every later deposit for that key is just a top-up.

Staking protocols lean on that.
They send a small deposit, wait for the validator to appear with the right credentials, then send the rest.
If someone with the validator key front-runs them, the worst case has always been a validator with the wrong credentials, which the protocol can detect before sending real money.

Glamsterdam adds a one-time builder onboarding at the fork.
If a pending deposit with builder credentials (the 0x0b prefix) sits in the queue at the fork, other pending deposits for the same key become top-ups for the builder, not the validator.

So a third outcome appears - no validator at all, and the ETH is credited to a builder.

Lido proposed a small spec fix, and client teams said no.
Their reasons were boring and correct.
Sepolia had already forked on this spec.
Hoodi releases were being cut.

A late change means re-testing, maybe re-forking Sepolia, and the risk that only some clients ship it, which is how you get a consensus split.
Instead, the plan is to test builder deposits and top-ups before the Hoodi fork.
The bug is narrow - it only touches deposits sitting in the queue at the fork moment.

A chain split is not narrow.

text:
I have always considered @milesgrimshaw one of the smartest investors in venture.

I remember Sept 2023, Miles came to our recording studio in London having just joined the @benchmark  partnership. At the time, he had done one deal; a small company called @LangChain.

Unknown to many but Miles raved about the founder @hwchase17. His excitement for the company was palpable.

Today the company is worth $1.2BN and serves 35% of the Fortune 500.

The other day I sat down with Harrison to discuss the big questions of the day and he allowed me to add my notes from the discussion below.

--

1. What Percent of Developer Salary Do You Spend on Coding Tools and How Has It Changed?

LangChain spends roughly 30% of its engineering salary on coding tools, a share that has fallen over the last two months even as token usage has gone up. The team tracks coding agent usage in LangSmith, sets budgets the VP of engineering can raise, and controls the harness. Its in-house cloud coding agent uses prompt caching and routing to cut costs.

What will this be in 12 months @BrendanFoody?

2. What Will Happen to the Inference Market?

Harrison says he underestimated the demand for inference and for coding agents, both far bigger markets than he expected three or four years ago. Echoing Eric Vishria's line that "Everything just works," he believes any inference provider will work, and he does not expect demand to drop anytime soon.

What does no one see about the inference market that everyone should see @spdholakia?

3. Why Harnesses Need to Be Neutral

Companies want to be able to switch models, but the harness can be tightly tied to a model, and context today is intricately linked to the harness. The harness connects the model to data, APIs and memory. If memory is built in a way that is linked to the harness, and the harness is linked to the model, the company ends up stuck.

Love to hear your thoughts on this one man @EnoReyes 

4. Why the Memory Layer Will Become More and More Important and How Instinct Crushed It

Memory is rare in agents today but will be incredibly common in the next few years. Instinct and Muse have nailed personalization and learning, so the product feels like it is for the individual user, through its tone or proactive follow-ups. Harrison still sees memory as super early.

What does no one see that everyone should see about the state of memory and where it goes @noahrshinn @mvernal?

5. Will We Have One Horizontal Agent or Tons of Vertical Agents in the Consumer Realm?

Consumers will have both, with horizontal agents interacting with vertical ones. Most apps should have a vertical agent because they can learn more about how a user interacts with them than a general agent can. Wrapping an app's many APIs in a single natural language agent also gives horizontal agents a better experience than raw APIs.

Love to hear your thoughts on this @FDavidsonT 

6. What Do Large Enterprises Care Most About Today?

Cost has risen as a concern for large enterprises, though it still ranks below accuracy and above latency. Security is a bigger concern for large enterprises but still sits below accuracy and cost.

7. Why Is Benchmark the Best Fund?

Benchmark invested in LangChain when it was just Harrison and Ankush, and the founders treated the firm as a third co-founder. As the company grew from two people to around 400, Benchmark has been its most consistent partner.

@chetanp what does no one know about how Benchmark works with founders that everyone should know?

text:
Ethereum is debating what to do with a deposit it wants to refuse, and the default answer is "burn it".

Two sides.
The proposal is EIP-8365, aimed at Hegota, the fork after Glamsterdam.
It stops new validators with 0x00 withdrawal credentials, the genesis-era type controlled by a BLS key with no execution address.

The EIP says that the population fell from about 600,000 to about 9,200, but 58 new ones were still created in 2026.
They can't use execution-layer exits, and if the BLS withdrawal key is lost, the balance is stranded on the consensus layer.
Every one of them also keeps old 0x00 code paths alive into the post-quantum transition.

Side one is the EIP as written.
When a pending deposit would create a new 0x00 validator, apply_pending_deposit just returns.
No validator, no refund, and the ETH stays locked in the deposit contract, the same treatment as a deposit with a bad signature. The check runs when the deposit is processed, not when it is sent.
So a deposit made before the fork that is still waiting in the entry queue after it gets skipped too.

Side two came up on Thursday's ACDC #189 call.
@BarnabasBusa suggested letting these validators in, but with no duties and no rewards, so the owner can still change credentials or exit.
Devs also discussed moving the check to when the deposit request is made, so anything submitted under the old rules is judged by the old rules.

Nothing was decided, and the review continues.
If you run deposit tooling or a staking backend, do you validate withdrawal credentials before you send the 32 ETH, or do you trust the consensus layer to tell you later? ;)

text:
The core step of a quantum attack on Bitcoin and Ethereum now fits in under 900 logical qubits within Google's gate budget. In three published attack designs, the machine would shrink by zero to about 28%.

On October 13, Jieyi Long of Theta Labs posted an 893-qubit circuit to ECDSA Fail, an open benchmark for the point addition that Shor's algorithm repeats to recover a private key. A day later he posted an 874-qubit version. Both stay below the 1,175 qubits and 2.7 million Toffoli gates Google proved for its own circuit in March.

Narrower circuits exist, down to 676 qubits, but all of them exceed Google's gate count. The 676-qubit one needs about 150 times as many.

Pierre-Luc Dallaire-Demers, a co-author of the ECDSA Fail paper, put the physical saving at 25% for the IonQ, Oratomic and Google attack designs. I checked each one.

- Google: about a quarter, if every part of the machine shrank with the qubit count.

- Oratomic: nothing with its published codes, and at most 16% with a code sized for 893 qubits.

- IonQ: about 28% fewer ions, but longer attempts, because the circuit needs about 1.6 times IonQ's Toffoli gates per addition.

Nobody has compiled a full attack around either circuit yet.
